note: Synthesised from per-sign recipes, not recorded.

imperial.note: The chancery Aramaic of the Achaemenid empire, and behind it the language of the bowls — with the pharyngeals, emphatics and uvular qoph that Modern Hebrew has lost, and with the letter names in their Aramaic rather than Hebrew shapes. Nothing Aramaic was ever recorded; every value here is reconstructed from Syriac spelling and from Hebrew and Arabic cognates. Arabic does most of the consonantal work because it is the only living language with the full set; Spanish, Italian and German are borrowed where Arabic's three vowels will not reach.

0.why: Arabic script is the only one available that writes a true glottal stop: آ, alef with madda, is [ʔaː], and ف supplies the spirantised final of ʾālap̄. Carmit would give the modern Hebrew name and let the initial ʾ dissolve into a plain vowel onset.
0.compromise: No Aramaic speech survives; the name is reconstructed from Syriac ʾālaph and its Hebrew and Arabic cognates. Arabic stress and vowel colour are imposed on it. The final [f] assumes begadkepat spirantisation was already operating — in the earliest Imperial Aramaic it may still have been a plain [p].

1.why: Castilian z is a genuine interdental [θ] — the spirantised taw of bēṯ — and Spanish e is a pure close-mid [e]. Arabic could give the [θ] with ث but has no [eː] and would force bīth; an English 'beth' would give a laxer [ɛ] and an aspirated onset that Aramaic did not have.
1.compromise: A reconstruction, not a recording: the value comes from Syriac bēṯ and from the begadkepat rule, and no Aramaic speaker is on tape. Spanish marks no vowel length, so the slow rate is a crude stand-in for the long [eː]. Modern Hebrew has lost this final [θ] entirely and says bet.

2.why: Italian gh before i is a hard unaspirated [g] with no palatalisation, and Italian vowels are pure. Arabic is no use here at all: in the Saudi standard ج is [dʒ], and there is no [g] in the inventory.
2.compromise: Reconstructed from cognates; nothing Aramaic is recorded. The Syriac form of this name is gāmal, not gimel — the hall prints Gimel and the clip follows the hall. Italian does not mark vowel length, so the [iː] is short. The letter's spirantised value after a vowel, [ɣ], is not shown by the name.

3.why: Spanish gives a dental stop [d] in initial position, pure [a] and [e], and a word-final Castilian z that is reliably [θ] — the spirantised taw of dālaṯ. No single Arabic string can produce [d] + [e] + [θ] together.
3.compromise: Reconstruction, not recording: Aramaic phonology here is inferred from Syriac dālaṯ and the Hebrew cognate. Spanish marks no length, so the stressed [aː] is short. Whether the second vowel was [e] or [a] — dāleṯ or dālaṯ — varies between the traditions.

4.why: German is the only convenient source of a real initial [h] followed by a long close [eː]: Spanish and Italian h is silent, and English 'hay' diphthongises to [heɪ].
4.compromise: Reconstructed from the Syriac and Hebrew names; no Aramaic recording exists. German gives the syllable its own falling contour, and whether the Aramaic name was hē or hā is not settled. The hall notes this letter is often silent at the end of a word, which a letter-name clip cannot show.

5.why: Arabic و is [w], and واو is the Arabic name of the very same inherited letter — one of the few cases where a living language simply has the word already, so the reading is guaranteed rather than coaxed.
5.compromise: Still a reconstruction: that Aramaic waw was [w] and not [v] is an inference from Syriac, from Greek transcriptions and from the Arabic cognate, not from any recording. Arabic واو has a long first vowel, [waːw], where the Aramaic name was probably short. Later Jewish reading turned this consonant into [v], which is what the modern system gives.

6.why: Arabic ز is an unambiguous [z] and ي after a fatha gives a clean [j] glide. Spanish z would give [θ] and Italian z would give [ts] — both catastrophically wrong for this letter.
6.compromise: Reconstructed from cognates; no Aramaic is recorded. The Arabic spelling forces a long [aː] where the name's first vowel was probably short. The Syriac name is zayn, a single syllable — the helping vowel in Zayin may be a Hebrew development that Aramaic did not share.

7.why: ح is the voiceless pharyngeal fricative the hall describes, made deep in the throat, and ث supplies the spirantised final [θ]. No other installed voice can make a pharyngeal of any kind — the nearest substitutes, Spanish j or Russian х, are velar or uvular and would misteach the letter.
7.compromise: A reconstruction: Aramaic ḥeth is known to have been pharyngeal from Syriac, Arabic and the Greek transcriptions, never from a recording. Arabic script has no [eː] — ي gives [iː] — so this is closer to ḥīth than ḥēth. That error is at least in the direction of a real tradition, since Eastern Syriac says ḥīth. Mandaic, as the hall notes, lost the sound altogether.

8.why: Arabic ط is the emphatic [tˤ] — pharyngealised, tongue drawn back, exactly the articulation the hall states — with ث for the spirantised final. No European voice has any emphatic consonant at all.
8.compromise: Reconstruction, not recording. Two problems. The vowel: Arabic gives [iː] for [eː], for want of a mid vowel in the script. And the emphasis: Arabic realises emphatics as pharyngealised, while the rival reconstruction, supported by Ethiopic and by Proto-Semitic comparison, makes them ejective [tʼ]. Nothing Aramaic survives to decide between them, so this clip commits to the Arabic realisation because it is the only one obtainable.

9.why: Arabic ي is a clean [j] and ذ is a true voiced interdental [ð] — the spirantised daleth of yōḏ. Spanish would give [ʝ] for the glide and lenite or drop the final d; English would diphthongise the vowel.
9.compromise: Reconstructed from Syriac yōḏ and the Hebrew cognate; no Aramaic is recorded. Arabic cannot write [oː] — و after a damma is [uː] — so what this clip actually says is yūdh. The consonants are right and the vowel is plainly wrong, which is the honest trade here: this letter is worth having for its final [ð], a sound Modern Hebrew has lost.

10.why: كاف is the Arabic name of the same inherited letter and comes out [kaːf] without any coaxing: a long [aː], an unaspirated [k], and the spirantised [f]. An English voice would aspirate the initial k.
10.compromise: Reconstruction rather than recording, though a well-supported one — Syriac kāp̄ and Arabic kāf agree. The only real assumption is that begadkepat spirantisation had already made the final [f] rather than [p] by the period the hall describes.

11.why: One Arabic word supplies everything: [l], a long [aː], and ذ for the spirantised daleth of lāmaḏ. Spanish and Italian have no [ð] that survives in final position.
11.compromise: Reconstructed from Syriac lāmaḏ and the Hebrew cognate; nothing Aramaic is recorded. Arabic velarises its l in some environments — the dark l of Allāh — but before [aː] here it should be the plain clear [l] wanted. Arabic stress falls on the heavy first syllable, which is probably where the Aramaic had it.

12.why: German eh is a long close [eː] set between two [m]s. Arabic would force mīm; Spanish and Italian would give a short vowel with no length contrast available.
12.compromise: Reconstruction from cognates, and here the cognates disagree: Syriac and Arabic both have mīm, while the form mēm follows the Hebrew and this hall's spelling. Which vowel the Imperial scribes said is not recoverable. The slow rate is holding a vowel that German would already lengthen.

13.why: نون is the Arabic name of the same letter and reads out as [nuːn] — a long [uː] between two clean dental nasals, with no substitution required anywhere.
13.compromise: Still a reconstruction in principle — no Aramaic is recorded — but Syriac nūn and Arabic nūn agree exactly, so there is nothing here to compromise on segmentally. The hall's remark that nun assimilates readily to a following consonant is a fact about the letter in words, not about its name, and the clip cannot show it.

14.why: Spanish j is a velar-to-uvular fricative [x~χ] — the spirantised kaph that ends this name — and Spanish surrounds it with the pure [a] and [e] that Arabic خ could not, since Arabic would wrap it in [i] or [u].
14.compromise: Reconstruction, not recording. The Syriac name of this letter is semkath, not samekh; the hall prints the Hebrew-shaped form and the clip follows it, so this is an Aramaic sound system applied to a Hebrew name-shape. Spanish marks no length on the [aː], and Spanish [x] is articulated slightly further forward than the Arabic خ this ought to be.

15.why: ع is the voiced pharyngeal the hall describes, and no other installed voice possesses it — Carmit drops the consonant entirely, which is precisely the loss the hall reports for later Jewish Babylonian Aramaic and for Mandaic. Arabic عاين is also a real word, so the reading is stable.
15.compromise: Reconstructed: the pharyngeal is inferred from Arabic, Syriac and Greek transcription practice, never heard. The Arabic spelling gives a long [aː] where the name is more likely [ˈʕajin] with a short vowel. And for the earliest period there is a live question whether ayin still stood apart from the inherited Proto-Semitic ghayin, which the alphabet does not distinguish.

16.why: Italian initial p is unaspirated, as a Semitic voiceless stop was; an English or German voice would give [pʰ], which is a different sound and the exact error the Greek hall exists to avoid. Arabic is no help — Modern Standard Arabic has no [p] at all.
16.compromise: Reconstruction from Syriac pē and the Hebrew cognate; no recording exists. Italian will not hold a final vowel long, so the slow rate stands in for the [eː], imperfectly. The letter's spirantised value [f], which the hall notes, is not shown by the name.

17.why: ص is the emphatic [sˤ] and ذ the voiced interdental [ð] — the two sounds this name needs, both present in one Arabic word and neither obtainable from any other installed voice. Modern Hebrew would give [ts], an affricate that is not the same sound at all.
17.compromise: Reconstructed, not recorded. Arabic gives [iː] for the final [eː]. The emphatic is rendered pharyngealised because that is what Arabic does; the rival reconstruction makes Aramaic emphatics ejective [sʼ], and no Aramaic evidence settles it. The hall prints Sadhe, with the spirantised [ð]; the Hebrew name Tsadi has neither the emphatic nor the fricative.

18.why: ق is a true uvular stop, formed far back in the mouth exactly as the hall describes, and ف gives the spirantised final. Modern Hebrew has merged qoph into kaph, so Carmit would give a plain [k] and destroy the one feature that makes this letter distinct.
18.compromise: Reconstruction from cognates; nothing Aramaic is recorded. [uː] again stands in for [oː], because the Arabic script has no [oː]. And whether Aramaic q was a voiceless uvular stop, as in Arabic, or an ejective [kʼ] as in Proto-Semitic and Ethiopic, is the same unsettled question that hangs over teth and sadhe.

19.why: Arabic ر is a true alveolar trill and ش a clean [ʃ]; ريش is an ordinary Arabic word, so the reading is reliable rather than coaxed out of nonsense. German would substitute its uvular [ʁ] and English would give an approximant.
19.compromise: Reconstructed, not recorded. The vowel comes out [iː], so the clip actually says rīš — which is the Eastern Syriac name, but not the form Resh the hall prints. And the consonant is genuinely open: the hall says 'rolled or uvular', and the Tiberian evidence that resh takes no doubling is usually read as pointing to a uvular articulation. This clip trills it, which is one of the two possibilities and not certainly the right one.

20.why: شين is the Arabic name of the same letter and reads as [ʃiːn] outright — the fricative and the long vowel both correct with no substitution.
20.compromise: A reconstruction in principle, but Syriac šīn and Arabic šīn agree and there is nothing to trade away segmentally. What the clip cannot show is the hall's real point about this letter: the unpointed square script writes both š and s with this one sign, and only the š value is voiced here.

21.why: Italian gives an unaspirated dental [t] and a genuine falling [au] diphthong — the same recipe the Greek hall uses for ταῦ. An English 'taw' would both aspirate the stop and monophthongise the diphthong to a long back vowel.
21.compromise: Reconstructed from Syriac taw and the Hebrew cognate; no Aramaic recording exists. Italian writes the second element as a full vowel [u] rather than the glide [w], so the name comes out marginally more disyllabic than it should. The letter's spirantised value [θ], which the hall notes, is not shown by the name — Modern Hebrew has lost that value and also says the name with a final [v], Tav.

22.why: Italian sc before e is [ʃ], and Italian genuinely doubles the nn — the geminate this name needs and which Spanish and German would both simplify. Arabic could geminate with shadda but would force [i] for the [e].
22.compromise: This is the one sign in the hall whose pronunciation is not a reconstruction: Mandaeans recite their alphabet, so the name is transmitted rather than inferred — though the vowel qualities of Mandaic as read in the community today are not necessarily those of the Sasanian period. The Italian works against it in one way: sce is inherently geminate in Italian, so the sh comes out held longer than it should be. The name is given in transliteration because the Mandaic spelling of the letter-name is not fixed.

modern.note: How these twenty-two glyphs are named today by the community that still writes them. This is Hebrew, not Aramaic surviving: the names are the Hebrew ones — Bet, Gimel, Dalet, Tsadi, Kuf, Tav against Beth, Gimel, Daleth, Sadhe, Qoph, Taw — and the phonology is Israeli, which has lost the pharyngeals, the emphatics and the uvular qoph. It earns the default click all the same, because Aramaic is read aloud in Jewish practice every day — the Kaddish, Kol Nidre, the Talmud, the Zohar — and it is read in exactly this voice. The strings are pointed so the voice cannot mistake a letter-name for the ordinary word it looks like.

0.why: Simply the Hebrew name of the letter.
0.compromise: The Aramaic name is Alaph, and the consonant should be a firm glottal stop; in Israeli Hebrew the aleph is usually no more than a vowel onset, which is the weakening the hall describes for later Aramaic. The final [f] the two names share is accidental agreement, not a shared rule.

1.why: The Hebrew name; the b is a plain stop.
1.compromise: The Aramaic name is Beth, ending in the spirantised [θ] that Israeli Hebrew has lost entirely. There is also a technical risk in this clip: unpointed, בית is the ordinary word bayit, 'house', and if the voice disregards the vowel points it will say bayit rather than bet.

2.why: The Hebrew name, with a hard [g].
2.compromise: The Aramaic and Syriac name is gāmal. The letter's fricative variant after a vowel, [ɣ], has been lost from Israeli Hebrew, so this name shows only the stop.

3.compromise: The Aramaic is Daleth, with the final [θ]; Israeli Hebrew ends it in a plain [t] and has also lost the letter's own fricative variant [ð], the 'th' of 'this' that the hall records.

4.why: The Hebrew name, a plain [h] and a short [e].
4.compromise: Close to the Aramaic hē apart from vowel length, which Israeli Hebrew does not mark. The letter's silence at the end of a word, where it marks a vowel, is not something a name-clip can show.

5.why: The Hebrew name, and Israeli Hebrew makes this letter [v].
5.compromise: This is the single loudest difference between the two systems. Ancient Aramaic waw is [w]; the Jewish reading turned it into [v], and the name changed with it. The hall's own entry says both.

6.why: The Hebrew name; [z] is one of the few consonants unchanged since antiquity.
6.compromise: Essentially none — this letter has moved less than any other. The Syriac name is the shorter zayn.

7.why: The Hebrew name. Israeli Hebrew realises this letter as a uvular fricative [χ].
7.compromise: Not the same sound as the Aramaic: [χ] is uvular, made at the back of the tongue, where Aramaic ḥeth is a pharyngeal [ħ] made in the throat. Some Mizrahi speakers still keep the pharyngeal, but the general Israeli voice — and this synthesiser — does not. Comparing this clip with the Arabic one in the reconstruction is the clearest way to hear what was lost.

8.why: The Hebrew name; the letter is now a plain [t].
8.compromise: The emphasis is gone. Israeli Hebrew has merged teth with taw, so this is indistinguishable from a plain t, where Aramaic ṭeth is articulated with the tongue drawn back.

9.why: The Hebrew name, with a clean [j] and [o].
9.compromise: The Aramaic is Yodh, ending in the spirantised [ð]; Israeli Hebrew has a plain [d]. The vowel, at least, is the [o] the Aramaic wants and which the Arabic script in the reconstruction could not supply.

10.compromise: Almost identical to the Aramaic kāp̄ apart from vowel length. Israeli Hebrew does keep this letter's fricative variant, [χ] rather than the older [x], which is why the hall's 'ch of loch' still means something to a Hebrew reader.

11.compromise: The Aramaic is Lamedh, with the spirantised [ð] at the end; Israeli Hebrew gives a plain [d].

12.compromise: None beyond vowel length, which Israeli Hebrew does not mark. Syriac and Arabic both call this letter mīm rather than mēm.

13.why: The Hebrew name, which is also the Aramaic and the Arabic one.
13.compromise: None beyond length. This letter's name has survived unchanged across the whole Semitic family.

14.why: The Hebrew name, ending in the fricative kaph [χ].
14.compromise: Israeli [χ] is uvular where the Aramaic spirantised kaph was velar [x], a small difference. The Syriac name of this letter is quite different: semkath.

15.why: The Hebrew name. In general Israeli Hebrew the letter itself is silent.
15.compromise: The consonant is simply absent. Aramaic ayin is a voiced pharyngeal made by constricting the throat; here there is nothing before the vowel at all. That silence is not a defect of the clip but the thing it is showing — the hall records the same loss in later Jewish Babylonian Aramaic and in Mandaic, where the letter became a plain vowel.

16.why: The Hebrew name, with the stop value of the letter.
16.compromise: Close to the Aramaic pē apart from length. Israeli Hebrew keeps this letter's fricative variant [f], so the alternation the hall describes is still live here, unlike beth's or daleth's.

17.why: The Hebrew name, with the affricate [ts].
17.compromise: Two changes at once. The name is Hebrew — the Aramaic is Sadhe, with a spirantised [ð] in the middle — and the sound has become an affricate [ts] where Aramaic had an emphatic fricative [sˤ]. Neither the emphasis nor the [ð] survives.

18.compromise: The uvular articulation is gone: Israeli Hebrew has merged qoph with kaph, so this is a plain [k] and the letter is now audibly indistinguishable from kaph. The Aramaic name is Qoph, with a [q] formed far back in the mouth and an [o].

19.why: The Hebrew name. Israeli Hebrew r is a uvular [ʁ].
19.compromise: The hall says the Aramaic r was 'rolled or uvular' and does not choose; Israeli Hebrew is firmly uvular, so this clip happens to voice one of the two live possibilities, though by a European route rather than an inherited one.

20.why: The Hebrew name, identical to the Aramaic and Arabic.
20.compromise: None beyond length. As in the reconstruction, only the š value of this two-valued sign is heard.

21.compromise: The Aramaic name is Taw, with a [w]; Israeli Hebrew ends it [v], by the same shift that turned waw into vav. The letter's fricative variant [θ] has also been lost from Israeli Hebrew, though Yemenite and Ashkenazi traditions preserve reflexes of it.

22.why: There is no Hebrew reading of this sign to give: dushenna is a Mandaic ligature and belongs to the Mandaic alphabet, not the square script. Its living pronunciation is the Mandaean one, so the same recipe is used in both systems — Italian sc before e is [ʃ] and Italian truly doubles the nn.
22.compromise: This entry is not a Hebrew reading at all, and is repeated from the reconstruction so that no sign in the hall is silent. Italian makes sce inherently geminate, so the sh is held longer than it should be. The name itself is genuinely transmitted rather than reconstructed — Mandaeans recite their alphabet — but the modern recitation's vowels are not guaranteed to be the ancient ones.
